raw_response:
I found seven catalogue-discovered candidates. The application suggestions below are design transfers, not claims of Rust compatibility or demonstrated deployment benefit. Dates are relative to 2014-06-11.

1. Ruby I18n public API with replaceable backends — https://guides.rubyonrails.org/v4.1.0/i18n.html
A stable translate/localize interface with replaceable backends lets localization grow independently of basic formatting and the core language. The Simple backend has explicit English-oriented limits, so richer requirements still need appropriate extensions. Pre-decision evidence: the version 4.1.0 guide, with Rails 4.1 dated April 2014 by the official release navigation.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/oh-jon-paul/awesome-i18n

2. ECMA-402 first-edition internationalization API — https://norbertlindenberg.com/2012/12/ecmascript-internationalization-api/index.html
A separately adoptable internationalization API supplies explicit locale-aware services without coupling their evolution to the next core-language release. Its first edition leaves resource loading and message construction to other layers. Pre-decision evidence: the original participant article dated 2012-12-18; the linked specification request failed.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/mrhota/awesome-i18n

3. ICU MessageFormat — https://unicode-org.github.io/icu/userguide/format_parse/messages/
A dedicated message library can handle complete translated sentences and plural/select branches while accepting parameters formatted separately. This suggests keeping grammatical message assembly outside basic formatting syntax. Library and locale-data integration remain necessary. Date status: unknown for the full documented behavior; early ICU availability does not date every feature in this live guide.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/mrhota/awesome-i18n

4. Unicode CLDR — https://cldr.unicode.org/
Keeping locale data in a separately released repository allows a localization library to update cultural conventions without changing core formatting syntax. It supplies a data boundary, not application translations or a complete runtime. Pre-decision availability: the official release index at https://cldr.unicode.org/index/downloads dates CLDR 25 to 2014-03-19; current feature coverage is not all backdated.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/mrhota/awesome-i18n

5. Jed — https://messageformat.github.io/Jed/
Separate locale catalogues can select messages using context and plural rules before a basic formatter interpolates reordered arguments. This provides a concrete lookup-then-interpolation division. Applications still supply converted catalogues and plural metadata. Date status: unknown; the opened primary documentation is undated.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/oh-jon-paul/awesome-i18n

6. messageformat — https://github.com/messageformat/messageformat
Compiling message patterns into functions could move plural/gender-aware message processing into optional application tooling and runtime libraries. The verified packages separate compilation, parsing, loading, and runtime dependencies. Transfer caveat: this is JavaScript tooling, and its currently documented packages were not dated before the cutoff. Date status: unknown.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/oh-jon-paul/awesome-i18n

7. Globalize — https://github.com/globalizejs/globalize
Optional formatting modules and separately loaded locale data let applications pay for the localization capabilities they need. Reusable or precompiled formatters provide another application-library boundary. Applications must manage module/data compatibility; this is a JavaScript design example. Date status: unknown for the current README's features.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/oh-jon-paul/awesome-i18n

The two opened awesome lists are live catalogues; their existence or contents at the decision cutoff was not established.
Unknown means historical feature availability was not established; post_decision=false with date_status=unknown is not a claim of pre-cutoff availability.
Current MDN content and ICU 79 release material were explicitly treated as later evidence. They were navigation or verification context, not pre-cutoff proof.
Seven fetch attempts failed, including retries. No content was inferred from failed pages or from search snippets alone.
The original ECMA-402 participant article is the successful historical verification source; the first-edition specification endpoint failed.

CLDR 25 has an official historical release date, but its old release page failed; the candidate's pre-decision classification covers the versioned data-component availability, not every modern CLDR feature.
No bindings, benchmarks, integrations, deployment claims, or usefulness claims were tested.
No recognized target-proposal exposure occurred; pretraining memory leakage cannot be ruled out.
